title.en: The Mental Health Crisis on Campus

stages.source_description: Part 1: Introduction (Slides 1-3: hook noticing the people around you, SDG 3 covers mental health, campus life beneath the surface)

A2.text: Look around this room for a moment. About one in four students here may feel more stress than they show. That is not a guess, because surveys tell us so.

B1.text: Take a moment and look around this room. Statistically, about one in four students here is carrying more stress than they let on. Researchers have actually measured this, not guessed at it.

B2.text: A quarter of the people sitting in a room like this one, statistically speaking, are carrying more psychological strain than their expression ever reveals. That figure is not intuition, but the result of actual measurement.

title.en: SDG 3 Means More Than the Body

A2.text: SDG 3 is the goal for good health and well-being. It is not only about the body. It also means care for the mind too. Taiwan takes both parts seriously.

B1.text: SDG 3 establishes the global objective of good health and well-being, and it covers the mind as much as the body. Taiwan has taken that seriously in law. This talk asks whether practice matches the promise.

B2.text: SDG 3 establishes a single global objective, and mental wellbeing sits inside that objective exactly as firmly as physical health does. Taiwan has enshrined that principle in law, though whether daily practice matches the promise is another matter entirely.

A2.text: University life can look easy from the outside. Classes, clubs and friends fill your schedule every day. But under the surface, many students carry a heavy weight.

B1.text: University life can look effortless from the outside, full of classes, clubs and friends. Underneath that surface, though, many students are quietly carrying a heavy weight. This talk is about what that weight actually looks like.

B2.text: From outside, a university schedule reads as nothing but classes, clubs and friends. What that timetable hides is the weight a considerable number of students are quietly carrying underneath it.

stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...
stages.source_description: Part 2: Problem (Slides 4-6: the scale of depressive tendency among university students, where the pressure comes from, the youth mortality figures that make this urgent)

A2.text: Here is a real number. In a 2024 survey, 23.1 percent of university students showed signs of depression. That share has grown over the past ten years.

B1.text: A 2024 survey of university students found that 23.1 percent showed signs of depression. That share, researchers noted, has been climbing for roughly a decade. School stress and money worries topped the list of causes.

B2.text: According to a 2024 national survey, 23.1 percent of university students showed signs of depression, and that figure has been rising steadily for roughly ten years. Heavy coursework and money strain were named most often as the top causes.

A2.text: Where does this stress come from? Most students point to school and money. Older students feel it the most, right before they must plan their future.

B1.text: Ask students where the pressure comes from, and two answers stand out: schoolwork and money. Third-year students report the biggest load of all, right before they have to plan their entire future.

B2.text: Coursework and money dominate whenever students are actually asked about the source of their pressure. Those in their third year carry the single heaviest load of anyone, arriving precisely when an entire future must also be planned.

A2.text: Here is a hard fact. Among people aged 15 to 24, self-harm is now the second leading cause of death. This is why the rest of this talk matters.

B1.text: One statistic is uncomfortable to hear, but silence would make the situation worse. Among those between 15 and 24, deaths linked to self-harm now rank as the second leading cause. That is why this talk exists.

B2.text: This next figure is difficult, but leaving it unsaid would be worse. Among Taiwanese aged 15 to 24, self-harm has become the second most common cause of death, and everything else in this talk follows from that single, sobering fact.

stages.source_description: Part 3: Achievements (Slides 7-9: the counselor-ratio law finally changes, the 1925 hotline, psychological leave now exists on paper)

A2.text: Good news: the law has changed. Schools must now have one counselor for every 900 students, not 1,200. That means more trained help for students like you.

B1.text: The law has finally caught up here. Universities must now provide one professional counselor for every 900 students, down from 1,200. That change alone should mean real, trained help for students like you.

B2.text: Legislation has finally caught up with demand in this area. The required counselor-to-student ratio at universities has moved from one in 1,200 to one in 900, a transition that should put genuine, trained support within significantly easier reach.

A2.text: Please remember one number: 1925. It is a free hotline, open all day and all night, every day of the year. Someone is always there to listen.

B1.text: One number is worth memorising: 1925. It connects you to a free, 24-hour hotline that has quietly grown busier every year since it launched. Someone is always there on the other end, ready to listen.

B2.text: If you remember only one single number from this entire talk, make it 1925. Since its establishment, this free, round-the-clock hotline has grown substantially busier with each passing year, and someone consistently, reliably answers it, day or night.

A2.text: Many schools now offer a program called psychological leave. It lets a stressed student take real time off, without shame. That option exists, right now, on your campus.

B1.text: Psychological leave now exists on paper at many schools. It gives a struggling student the choice to step back, without any stigma. Whether students actually use it is another question, one the next few slides explore.

B2.text: A formal policy called psychological leave already sits in most university handbooks, letting any struggling student step back without shame. What remains unclear is whether students actually use that right, a question the next few slides take up directly.

stages.source_description: Part 4: Solutions (Slides 10-12: hiring enough counselors, making help easier to reach, campus-wide prevention instead of waiting for crisis)

A2.text: The new law sounds simple: hire more counselors. But schools need real money to pay them well. Without that money, the new rule stays just words on paper.

B1.text: On paper, fixing the ratio looks easy: simply hire more staff. Turning that into reality costs considerable money, though, and schools without enough budget will struggle to keep the new positions filled.

B2.text: Hiring more staff sounds like a simple fix on paper. Converting that instruction into an actual, funded position is another matter entirely, and schools without adequate budget will struggle to keep those positions staffed for long.

A2.text: Help should not be hard to find. Instead of one fixed office hour, universities could offer evening slots, online chat, or a quiet drop-in room. Easier access saves lives.

B1.text: Nobody stuck in a crisis should have to wait for a scheduled appointment slot. Evening hours, an online chat line or a quiet drop-in space would all lower that wait. Easier access can genuinely save lives.

B2.text: A single, fixed office hour is an oddly restrictive gate for something this time-sensitive. Evening slots, an online chat option or a confidential drop-in space would each widen that gate considerably, and a wider gate saves lives.

title.en: Instead of Waiting for a Crisis

A2.text: Instead of waiting for a crisis, schools can act early. Classes can teach students to notice stress in themselves and their friends. Small lessons now can prevent big pain later.

B1.text: Rather than waiting for a crisis, universities can build prevention into normal classes. Teaching students to notice warning signs in themselves and their friends could spare someone real pain later.

B2.text: Instead of merely reacting once a crisis has already occurred, universities can intervene earlier. Courses can teach students to recognise stress in themselves and in their friends, well before it escalates into something harder to manage.

stages.source_description: Part 5: Implications (Slides 13-16: one continuous tension — a law that outruns its budget, access that is not the same as trust, a leave nobody takes, and why both structural and cultural fixes are needed together)

title.en: If the Law Outruns the Budget
title.zh: 如果法規跑在預算前面

A2.text: Here is the problem. If schools cannot fill these new counselor jobs, the better ratio only exists on paper. Low pay and short contracts make this job hard to keep.

B1.text: If these new positions stay unfilled, the improved ratio would exist only on paper. It would not yet exist in the room. Low pay on a one-year contract is usually why counselors are hard to keep.

B2.text: Funding a position and filling it are two different things entirely. Low pay on a one-year contract makes these new counselor roles a hard sell, and an unfilled seat keeps the better ratio just a number on paper.

title.en: Access Is Not the Same as Trust

A2.text: More counselors are not the whole answer. Many people still stay away, even when help is right there. They worry about time, distance, or simply being seen.

B1.text: More counselors alone will not solve this problem completely. A large share of students who could genuinely benefit stay away, even when help is there. Time, distance and privacy worries all get in the way.

B2.text: Simply adding counselors does not resolve the underlying problem. Many students capable of benefiting nonetheless avoid the office, even with help located down the corridor. It is privacy that concerns them most, followed closely by time and distance.

A2.text: Psychological leave exists at many schools. Yet only about 7.5 percent of students have ever used it. A right on paper is not the same as a right people use.

B1.text: Very few students take the psychological leave on the books. Roughly 7.5 percent actually do, according to one count. Having a right on paper is not the same as feeling free enough to use it.

B2.text: Only a small fraction of students, roughly 7.5 percent by one estimate, ever actually use the psychological leave written into university policy. Possessing that right on paper does not translate into feeling safe enough to exercise it.

A2.text: So we have two gaps, not one. Schools need enough trained staff, and students need to feel safe asking for help. Closing only one gap will not be enough.

B1.text: Two separate gaps sit side by side here. One is about capacity, enough trained staff, and the other is about comfort, feeling safe enough to ask. Fixing only one genuinely leaves the other wide open.

B2.text: Two distinct gaps operate here simultaneously, not one. Capacity concerns whether enough trained staff exist at all, while comfort concerns whether students feel safe enough to approach them, and addressing only one leaves the other exactly as wide as before.

stages.source_description: Part 6: Call to action (Slides 17-20: summary of progress and gaps, students do not need a perfect system, learn the signs and the number, reaching out is not weakness)

title.en: Progress, and What It Is Missing

A2.text: Let's look at where we stand. Taiwan has a better law, a free hotline, and real leave rules. But staffing and stigma still hold this progress back.

B1.text: Take stock of the complete picture for a moment. Taiwan can now point to a stronger law, a working hotline and genuine leave policies. Yet staffing gaps and quiet stigma keep pulling that progress backward.

B2.text: Taken together, the picture is genuinely encouraging: a stronger law, a working hotline, and leave policies written on the books. It is stigma that continues to drag this progress backward, quietly, far more than any remaining staffing gap.

title.en: You Do Not Need a Perfect System
title.zh: 你不需要一個完美的系統

A2.text: You do not need a perfect system to help someone today. If a friend seems different, ask how they really are. That question can matter more than you think.

B1.text: Nobody is asking you to fix the entire system by tomorrow. Simply noticing that a friend seems different and asking how they are doing counts as something real. A sincere question can matter a great deal.

B2.text: This talk is not asking you to repair the entire system by tomorrow. A friend who suddenly seems different, met with one sincere, well-timed question, already represents meaningful action, sometimes even a life-changing one.

title.en: Learn the Signs, Say the Number

A2.text: Learn to notice the early signs: less sleep, low energy, or pulling back from friends. Then remember one number, 1925, and say it out loud. It could help someone you love.

B1.text: Warning signs are often genuinely subtle: less sleep, less energy, gradually drifting away from friends. Knowing them matters, but so does knowing the number to call afterward, 1925. Saying it out loud could genuinely help.

B2.text: Warning signs rarely announce themselves loudly: reduced sleep, fading energy, a quiet, gradual drift away from friends. Recognising them is only half of it, though, since knowing which number to say immediately afterward, 1925, can genuinely change what happens next.

A2.text: It is not weakness to ask for help. It is strength, and help exists right now, totally free. If you need it, call 1925, day or night.

B1.text: Reaching out for help is not weakness. It is strength, and it takes genuine courage to admit that you are struggling. Help exists right now, completely free, and one number connects you to it: 1925.

B2.text: Weakness is not the right word for reaching out, since what it actually takes is courage, the courage to admit that something is genuinely difficult right now. Support is there, entirely free of charge, one phone call away: 1925.
